extracted.intended_audience: screenwriting students, script analysts, and practicing screenwriters
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and analytic criteria for how character is constructed and perceived in screenplays, with emphasis on action (praxis), non‑verbal/verbal behavior, habitual action, characterization, environment, and how these relate to premise and subtext.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character as a narrative agent / 'storyworld participant'
rubrics_metrics.description: Narratologist Uri Margolin defines a character as a “storyworld participant” or narrative agent — a participant who causes and/or experiences the events that define a narrative and orients reader attention and understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat characters as agents whose actions produce and structure plot; analysis should focus on what characters do (their role in events) rather than treating them as biographical personhood alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Praxis (action) as the primary function of character
rubrics_metrics.description: The function of character in dramatic narrative is best understood through praxis (πρᾶξις) — the deeds or actions of a person; audiences know a character’s morality (ethos) and reasoning (dianoia) only via their actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write scenes that reveal character through behavior and choices; in screenwriting, interior states should be shown by what characters do rather than explained directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Micro vs. Macro action
rubrics_metrics.description: Action operates on macro and micro scales: macro actions are overt decisions (sacrifices, cheating, car chases); micro actions are subtle behaviors (a glance, taking off a hat) that can destabilize equilibrium and carry powerful subtext.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use both scales strategically: macro actions for clear turning points and stakes; micro actions to reveal subtext, nuance, and to convey character without exposition (William Goldman / Raymond Chandler example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-verbal behavior (kinesics, haptics, proxemics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non‑verbal modes include kinesics (body movements, gestures, facial expression, glance), haptics (touch behavior), and proxemics (spatial relationships); these communicate feelings, social status, power relations and relationship dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In scripts, use non‑verbal cues (stage directions) to show social roles, power, attraction/repulsion and relationship changes; categorize touch and proxemic zones appropriately (intimate/personal/social/public) to create meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paralanguage (intonation, emphasis) — use sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Paralanguage includes intonation, emphasis, and stress; while actors often dislike line‑reading cues, paralanguage can be a useful dramatic tool when used sparingly and appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-prescribing vocal delivery in screenplay text, but include selective paralanguage when it is essential to the scene’s subtext (example: When Harry Met Sally — the shift back to normal voice communicates emotional change).

rubrics_metrics.name: Active dialogue as praxis vs. didactic/on-the-nose dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue can function as action: 'active dialogue' is context-driven, a contest for power or persuasion that reveals character; 'didactic' or on-the-nose speeches simply state inner states and undermine dramatic action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write conversations as exchanges of competing intentions and actions (a dialectic) — treat dialogue as an active form of praxis. Avoid speeches that merely report feelings or lesson the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habitual action for exposition and equilibrium
rubrics_metrics.description: Habitual actions establish the initial equilibrium of a character’s life (routine behaviors) and serve exposition; they can also be the subject matter for entire films (neorealist approach).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use habitual action in act one to ground a character and make later disequilibrium meaningful; consider whether habitual routines can themselves drive narrative (not only background texture).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization (observable qualities) vs. character-as-praxis
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterization is 'the sum of all observable qualities' (age, IQ, sex, style of speech, dress, occupation, personality, values), whereas character-as-praxis is what characters reveal through choices under pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance both: supply characterization details to enrich the actor’s palette and reader’s image, but ensure those traits manifest in choices and actions that propel the plot (McKee vs Egri debate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Environment as part of character (equilibrium and setting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Environment is more than habitat — it is the state of equilibrium surrounding a character; character and environment are closely interrelated and may function as one in narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use setting, props, wardrobe, and spatial organization to convey interior states and social conditions; don’t assume interiority must be shown only through action — environment can communicate preexisting dispositions and constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character must embody or oppose the script’s premise
rubrics_metrics.description: If a screenplay has a clear premise, the protagonist must either (a) personally hold that premise, or (b) hold an opposing premise; the antagonist should hold the opposite premise to create conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shape characters so their core beliefs align with or oppose the premise; have actions and learning across the plot test and potentially change those beliefs, ensuring motivation is belief-driven and plausibly develops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of subtext (behavioral subtext created by micro-actions and stage directions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subtext arises when behavior contradicts or complicates spoken words — micro-actions, gestures, pauses and stage directions create subtextual meaning beyond dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Layer script with small, deliberately placed non‑verbal beats and actions that contradict or deepen spoken lines; use stage directions to indicate pivotal micro-behaviors that shift power or reveal interior change (Han/Leia example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural contingency of non-verbal cues
rubrics_metrics.description: Some kinesic responses (micro-expressions) may be universal, but many non‑verbal behaviors (eye contact, gestures) are culturally conditioned and carry different meanings across cultures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of cultural variation when writing or analyzing non‑verbal behavior; avoid assuming a gesture or proxemic convention will read the same to all audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage directions and scene detail should support praxis without over-directing actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage directions in screenplays can richly communicate non‑verbal behavior (gaze, touch, facial expression) that produces subtext, but excessive prescription (especially of vocal delivery) can be resisted by actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write stage directions that clarify critical non‑verbal beats essential to story and subtext, but avoid over-prescribing performance; reserve detailed paralanguage and line‑reading cues for when they are dramatically necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: True character revealed under pressure — choices as revelation
rubrics_metrics.description: “TRUE CHARACTER … is revealed in the choices a human being makes under pressure — the greater the pressure, the deeper the revelation,” (McKee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design scenes with escalating pressure that force characters into revealing decisions; use those pressured choices as primary evidence of who the character truly is and to produce dramatic turning points.
